newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk Islamist Erbakan loses secularist battle.
newsitem.headline: Turk Islamist Erbakan loses secularist battle.

text.p: Turkey's first Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, who resigned on Wednesday to resolve a fierce row with the military, is a political maverick hounded from office by a hostile secularist elite.
Since taking power last June, Erbakan's unlikely coalition with conservatives had been locked in a bitter political war of attrition with secularists over his plans for Islamist reforms.

But the resolve shown in his chequered 28-year political journey to power, long obstructed by opposition from mainstream political rivals, suggests the veteran Welfare leader could emerge stronger from fresh polls.
"We got six million votes last time. If we had an election now we would get at least 10 million," Erbakan told foreign correspondents this week at a rare briefing.

Erbakan capitalised on disarray in the right-wing political establishment to win a narrow victory in 1995 general elections. Personal rivalries across the political spectrum opened the way for his coalition with pro-Western Tansu Ciller, who earlier served as Turkey's first woman prime minister.
Many voters were drawn by his promise of an economic revival and an improvement in Turkey's international profile.
He repeatedly espoused a vision of global Moslem brotherhood, going against the grain of Turkey's decades-long ambitions to get closer to Europe and the United States.
"The West learned everything it knows from the Moslems," he said in a newspaper interview before coming to office.
Erbakan visited Iran and Libya shortly after taking power in trips that angered Turkey's Western allies, who regard the two countries as rogue states.
Statements made by Erbakan subsequently reinforced concerns about his stated hostility to NATO and the European Union.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel nearly cancelled a visit to Ankara in March after Erbakan chided EU countries, saying they would "bow their heads when they talk with Turkey" about the cost of its customs union with the EU.
"The new world leader Turkey will receive the respect and treatment which it deserves," he told his party faithful.

But Erbakan remained largely powerless to prevent a blossoming of defence links between Turkey and Israel, at the behest of the Turkish military, that has drawn anger from Welfare supporters as well as many in the Arab world and Iran.
His resilience helped him withstand a constant stream of hostility from the secularist media, which he blamed for unseating the government by targeting him with "false agendas".
Last month a prosecutor called for the constitutional court to outlaw Erbakan's Welfare Party on grounds that it threatened Moslem but secular Turkey's basic principles of state.

"It has become clear that (Welfare) has become a focus of actions contrary to the principle of secularism in the constitution and has pushed our country towards a civil war atmosphere," said charges read out by prosecutor Vural Savas.
The prosecutor cited a warning from Erbakan that Welfare's rise to power could be "bloody" and a call for Moslems to join the party's jihad, or holy struggle.
The 70-year-old, who served as deputy prime minister in two coalition governments in the 1970s, managed to fight off a series of censure motions with a narrow margin in parliament.

His secularist coalition partners were seen as a major factor in preventing Erbakan from implementing the Islam-based theories he distilled during long years in opposition in a manifesto called the "Just Order".

Political and economic realities have undone manifesto vows to scrap interest rates and do away with "world imperialism and Zionism as well as Israel and a handful of champagne-drinking collaborators in the holding companies that feed it".

Last weekend he hosted the founding session of the Developing-8, an economic cooperation group of Moslem countries, but its own future looks shaky without Erbakan at the helm. The domestic economy, meanwhile, remains mired in deep public deficits and persistently high inflation.

Erbakan, a mechanical engineer, spent two years doing research at a West German university and working in factories in the Ruhr during the post-war reconstruction boom after graduating at the age of 22.
His time abroad did not distract him from his obligations as a Moslem -- he has been praying five times a day since the age of 13 -- nor impress him with the ways of the West.

He was born in the northern town of Sinop in 1926, one of six children of a father who had served as a travelling Islamic judge in the crumbling Ottoman Empire at the beginning of the century. Erbakan is married with three children.

He entered politics as an independent Islamist MP for the conservative city of Konya in 1969, accusing then prime minister Suleyman Demirel, now president, of removing him as head of a respected business group because of his beliefs.
